title: 3 things to know about how APAC power systems should adapt to LNG disruptions
gist: The Iran war has removed roughly a fifth of global LNG supply via the Strait of Hormuz, and Wood Mackenzie argues this is a multi-year Qatari export loss (Ras Laffan strikes), not a temporary price spike — meaning APAC utilities and developers need to permanently diversify supply routes and accelerate renewables-and-storage rather than wait for a return to normal.

themes.theme: Scale of the Hormuz/Gulf LNG shock

insights.claim: About 90% of LNG that transits the Strait of Hormuz flows east, meaning disruption to Gulf LNG supply caused by the war on Iran has disproportionately hit the Asia Pacific region rather than being evenly distributed globally.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: APAC gas-importing economies carry outsized exposure to this conflict relative to Western markets, a key regional risk-allocation signal for investors.
insights.quote: With 90% of LNG through the Strait of Hormuz flowing east, disruption to global LNG supplies caused by the war on Iran have disproportionately affected the Asia Pacific region.

insights.claim: At its peak, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz removed around 80 million tonnes per annum (mmtpa) of LNG from the market, roughly a fifth of global supply.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: An ~80 mmtpa peak loss is a scale investors can use to size global LNG price and margin impact versus prior supply-shock episodes.
insights.locator: at its peak, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz removed around 80 million tonnes

insights.claim: A country's exposure to the Gulf LNG shock is determined by market-specific factors — the role of gas in its generation mix and the diversity of its gas supply sources — rather than simply by the volume of LNG it imports.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Investors should map exposure by generation-mix and supply-diversity metrics per country, not headline import volumes, to correctly rank which APAC power markets are most at risk.
insights.locator: however, countries' individual exposure is determined by market-specific factors

insights.claim: Only one APAC country scores highly on both risk factors (high gas share of generation mix and low supply diversity), leaving it exposed to Gulf LNG at roughly seven times the cost of its domestic gas.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: A ~7x cost gap versus domestic gas is a concrete margin/cost-of-power shock for the single most exposed market, a candidate for the sharpest local power-price and fuel-switching moves.
insights.locator: leaving it vulnerable to Gulf LNG at roughly seven times the cost

themes.theme: A multi-year structural loss, not a price spike

insights.claim: Iranian strikes on LNG plants at Ras Laffan have removed significant Qatari export capacity for up to five years, meaning that even when the Strait of Hormuz reopens, LNG markets will not simply return to pre-war conditions.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Traders and utilities should stop pricing this as a transient spike and instead model a multi-year structural Qatari supply gap even after transit routes normalize.
insights.quote: Iranian strikes on LNG plants at Ras Laffan have removed significant Qatari export capacity for up to five years.
insights.locator: this is not a short-term price spike but a multi-year supply loss

insights.claim: Reopening the Strait of Hormuz will restore much of the LNG supply lost to the Asian market since March, but there will be no full 'back to normal' given the multi-year Qatari capacity loss.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: A Strait reopening should not be read by markets as a full resolution signal — a residual structural supply deficit will persist.
insights.locator: there will be no 'back to normal'

insights.claim: The LNG supply loss hit APAC markets precisely when regional power systems had the least flexibility to absorb a shortfall, because every grid in the region has faced record-temperature-driven peak loads, with the greatest risk backloaded into the second half of 2026.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: H2 2026 is flagged as the highest-risk window for APAC power reliability and price spikes, since some countries have not yet passed their peak cooling-demand season.
insights.locator: the risk is backloaded into the second half of 2026

themes.theme: Hedging response: diversification over more Gulf gas

insights.claim: In the face of a multi-year supply loss, the APAC markets that come out ahead will be those that prioritize improved power-system flexibility rather than simply importing more Gulf gas.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Investors should favor exposure to flexibility assets (storage, peaking, demand response) in APAC power over simple LNG import-capacity plays.
insights.locator: the winners will be markets that focus on improved flexibility

insights.claim: Route and counterparty diversification for LNG supply has shifted from being a cost-optimisation measure for utilities to being a security requirement.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: Expect APAC utilities to pay a diversification premium going forward — a structural change in procurement strategy, not a temporary hedge.
insights.quote: For utilities, route and counterparty diversification is now a security requirement rather than a cost-optimisation measure.
insights.locator: what it means: the need to hedge a lasting supply shock

insights.claim: The damage to gas economics from the Gulf LNG shock is likely to accelerate developers' renewables-and-storage project pipelines across the region.
insights.speaker: Nikhil Babu
insights.so_what: A geopolitical gas shock is being used by Wood Mackenzie as a structural catalyst for renewables-and-storage capex in APAC — a theme for clean-energy investors to track alongside the LNG story.
insights.locator: for developers, the impact on gas economics is likely to drive an accelerated renewables-and-storage pipeline
